issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette: David, a 53-year-old social worker from the Midwest, had spent most of his adult life helping others navigate difficult transitions. He was married, shared a modest home with his wife, and had a steady routine that began each day with a brisk walk through the neighborhood, checking the traffic lights and the bus schedule before heading to the county shelter where he spent his mornings. The first time he was a victim, he was in his late twenties, a student studying criminal justice. While walking home after a late lecture, a man he had met on campus stepped into his path. He stopped, turned to face him, and in a single motion lunged, grabbing David's shoulder and forcing his hands against his back. The assault was swift, brutal, and the man fled into a narrow alley that closed with a rusted metal door at its end. David was left shaking, the air cold and thick with the smell of alley trash, and he heard the echo of the stranger's footsteps fading into the night. The memory of that moment has never fully faded. Every time he recalls the grip on his shoulder, the sound of the alley door slamming, and the sudden darkness that swallowed the street, he feels an immediate surge of terror that is almost identical to the panic he felt then. Words fail him; he can only remember fragments-his hands clenched, the rough skin of the assailant, the metallic taste that lingers in his mouth. The shame that surfaces when he thinks of the violation is overwhelming, a feeling that it was his fault that something so awful could happen to him. This intrusive recollection is the starting point for a loop that has come to dominate David's daily life. The remembrance of the assault does not merely bring back the terror; it also fuels a heightened sense of threat. As soon as he thinks of the alley, his mind races to imagine that the same man might reappear, or that someone else could replicate the violence. This perception of danger triggers his first maladaptive strategy: avoidance of enclosed spaces. He now refuses to go through the downtown subway, the cramped stairwell at the shelter, or even the small meeting rooms he once used to discuss case plans. He replaces those spaces with wide, open halls, or the bright, airy windows of the community center. When his mind drifts toward the memory, the urge to suppress thoughts of the assault spikes; he finds himself deliberately pushing the images and sensations away, forcing himself to think about his work instead. The threat monitoring that follows each memory compels David to constantly check behind him, even on the flat sidewalk. He scans every direction, looking for a shadow or a shadowed figure, and his pulse quickens at the slightest movement in his periphery. The anxiety is so strong that it sometimes delays his work: a brief pause to ensure the alley doors are locked, a check to confirm the security cameras are operational, a hesitation before entering a room that feels too confined. The longer a task takes, the more he suspects that something bad is unfolding. He feels a knot in his stomach, convinced that any delay could invite danger. The anticipation of threat intensifies his avoidance, which, in turn, leaves him less able to confront the memory in a controlled way. The avoidance behaviors reinforce his sense of threat. When he avoids the subway, he feels as if he is retreating from a real danger; when he delays tasks because he is constantly on guard, he confirms his belief that the world is hostile. Each time he engages in threat monitoring, the memory resurfaces, reminding him that he was once in a place that felt both small and vulnerable. He believes that by staying alert, he is protecting himself, but the protective effort only solidifies the belief that threats are imminent. David's job as a social worker brings him into frequent contact with people who are in crisis, people who have experienced trauma, and people who speak about violence in their communities. In recent weeks he has felt the sting of his own trauma more acutely. During a session with a client who had been assaulted, David felt a surge of helplessness, and the memory of his own violation flooded back. He avoided the client's apartment because the apartment's narrow hallway reminded him of the alley. The avoidance caused friction with the client, who felt that David was not fully present. The fallout at work added a layer of shame that reinforced his sense that he had failed to keep his mind safe and his professional duties intact. After months of feeling trapped by the cycle, David finally reached a tipping point. The day after a client's sudden anger escalated into a crisis because he had perceived David's absence, David's wife asked him what was wrong. He could no longer pretend that the memory of the assault was merely a past event. He had been avoiding closed spaces for weeks, checking behind him constantly, delaying routine tasks, and suppressing the thoughts that would bring him to his knees. The culmination of those behaviors had left him exhausted, fearful of both the world and his own mind. When his wife gently encouraged him to seek help, David realized that staying silent would only prolong the terror. He was afraid that confronting the memory might unravel his ability to protect himself, yet he was also hopeful that a therapist could help him untangle the loop of memory, threat, and avoidance that had become his everyday reality.
